overview.text: The Labour Party is a major political party in the United Kingdom. It emerged from efforts by trade unionists and socialists to give working people representation in Parliament: the Labour Representation Committee formed in 1900, and its elected members adopted the Labour name in 1906. Ramsay MacDonald led the first Labour government in 1924, though it lacked a majority. After the Second World War, Clement Attlee’s Labour government established the National Health Service. The party has alternated in government and opposition with the Conservatives through much of modern British politics. Keir Starmer was elected Labour leader in 2020. Its history links organized labor, parliamentary elections, and debates over public services.

key_facts.text: The Labour Representation Committee formed in 1900.
Labour MPs adopted their party name after the 1906 election.
Ramsay MacDonald led the first Labour government in 1924.
Clement Attlee’s government introduced the National Health Service.
Keir Starmer was elected party leader in April 2020.

overview.text: Pakistan is a South Asian state that became independent in 1947 as British India was partitioned. Its capital is Islamabad, and its territory meets India, Afghanistan, Iran, and China, with an Arabian Sea coast. At independence, Pakistan had two geographically separated wings, West Pakistan and East Pakistan. Political conflict and war in 1971 led to the eastern wing becoming the independent state of Bangladesh. Pakistan’s present federation includes the provinces of Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as the Islamabad Capital Territory. The events of 1971 show that independence in 1947 did not settle questions of political representation between the country’s two wings.

key_facts.text: Pakistan became independent in August 1947.
Islamabad is Pakistan’s capital.
Pakistan borders India, Afghanistan, Iran, and China.
East Pakistan became Bangladesh after the 1971 war.
Pakistan has four provinces: Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

overview.text: The Thirty Years’ War was a series of connected conflicts fought from 1618 to 1648, centered on the Holy Roman Empire. It began amid a revolt by Protestant estates in Bohemia against Habsburg rule; the 1618 Defenestration of Prague became a symbol of its opening. The imperial and Catholic League victory at White Mountain in 1620 did not end the wider fighting. Other European powers entered, and dynastic and strategic aims joined disputes over religion. Armies and their movements devastated many communities. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended the war and reshaped political arrangements in central Europe. The conflict was neither one continuous battle nor simply a Catholic-versus-Protestant contest.

The 1618 Defenestration of Prague helped begin the Bohemian revolt.
Imperial and Catholic League forces won at White Mountain in 1620.
Other European powers joined for political as well as religious reasons.

overview.text: Sargon of Akkad was an early Mesopotamian ruler whose conquests joined previously rival city-states of Sumer under Akkadian rule. The period named for Agade, or Akkad, began around the middle of the third millennium BCE. Sargon took the title of king and campaigned beyond southern Mesopotamia, helping establish a territorial empire that outlasted him. His sons Rimush and Manishtushu succeeded him, while the empire later reached its height under his grandson Naram-Sin. The dynasty’s later campaigns extended its influence toward Anatolia, inner Iran, Arabia, and the Mediterranean. Sargon’s own conquests began a period of rule over multiple regions, though the empire’s greatest reach came after his reign.

key_facts.text: The Akkadian period is named after the city of Agade, also called Akkad.
Sargon conquered the rival Sumerian cities of southern Mesopotamia.
He also led campaigns farther east and north.
His sons Rimush and Manishtushu succeeded him.
The empire reached its apogee under Naram-Sin, Sargon’s grandson.

overview.text: The guillotine was a mechanical device for executing a condemned person by decapitation with a heavy blade. It became closely identified with the French Revolution after its adoption in 1792 and was used on people from very different social ranks. Joseph-Ignace Guillotin advocated a uniform method of execution, but he did not invent the machine that bears his name; the physician Antoine Louis designed it. Revolutionary figures executed by guillotine included Louis XVI in January 1793. The device was presented by reformers as a more reliable method than a sword or axe, although it remained a tool of capital punishment. France continued using it long after the revolutionary period.

key_facts.text: The guillotine was adopted for use in France in 1792.
Joseph-Ignace Guillotin advocated it but did not invent the device.
Antoine Louis designed the instrument.
Louis XVI was guillotined on 21 January 1793.
The Science Museum preserves guillotine blades from revolutionary France.

overview.text: Australia is both a sovereign country and the name used for the continental landmass at the center of its territory. It includes the mainland, Tasmania, and many smaller islands, with Canberra as national capital. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on these lands for tens of thousands of years. The modern Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901 when six British colonies federated into one country. The new federal system divided powers between national and state governments, while most First Nations people were excluded from the political process that created it. Australia’s history therefore joins a much older Indigenous past with a newer federal state and its continuing constitutional development.

key_facts.text: Australia includes a mainland and many surrounding islands.
Canberra was chosen as the capital site in 1908.
Six British colonies federated on 1 January 1901.
Most Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were excluded from the federation process.
The Constitution initially gave states primary responsibility for First Nations affairs.

overview.text: Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom with a long history as a separate kingdom. Its medieval rulers and communities maintained ties across Europe, including the alliance with France remembered as the Auld Alliance. In 1707, legislation passed in Edinburgh and Westminster joined the kingdoms of Scotland and England into Great Britain and created a shared Parliament. Scotland nevertheless retained distinctive legal and educational institutions. A devolved Scottish Parliament began meeting again in 1999 and makes laws in areas assigned to it, while the UK Parliament handles reserved matters. Edinburgh is Scotland’s capital. These different stages explain why Scotland is a country with its own institutions but is not an independent sovereign state today.

The 1707 Acts of Union created the Kingdom of Great Britain.
The union created one Parliament of Great Britain.
The Scottish Parliament first met again in May 1999.
The devolved Parliament makes laws on specified Scottish matters.

overview.text: The Alhambra Decree, also called the Edict of Expulsion, was issued by Ferdinand and Isabella at Granada on 31 March 1492. It ordered Jews living in their kingdoms and lordships to leave by the end of July and forbade their return. The document accused Jews of drawing converted Christians away from Catholic practice, reflecting the rulers’ religious policy rather than an established fact about Jewish communities. Jews faced exile or conversion to Christianity; both choices disrupted long-established families and communities. A contemporary Jewish account describes the losses and uncertainty of departure. The decree concerned Jews who had not converted, and it should be distinguished from later measures directed at Muslims.

It was issued in the names of Ferdinand and Isabella.
Jews were ordered to depart by the end of July 1492.
The decree barred their return under severe penalties.
A contemporary Jewish account describes the expulsion and some conversions.

overview.text: Shah Jahan ruled the Mughal Empire from 1628 to 1658 and is especially remembered for monumental architecture. After his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, he ordered the Taj Mahal, a marble mausoleum at Agra built by artisans from across the empire and beyond. He also established Shahjahanabad as a new capital at Delhi, with the Red Fort as its palace complex. These buildings combined imperial display with sophisticated garden planning, stonework, and decoration. His reign did not end through a normal succession: his son Aurangzeb forcibly displaced him in 1658. The Taj Mahal’s fame can obscure Shah Jahan’s broader role as a ruler and patron of Mughal urban architecture.

key_facts.text: Shah Jahan reigned from 1628 to 1658.
He commissioned the Taj Mahal in memory of Mumtaz Mahal.
The Taj Mahal stands at Agra beside the Yamuna River.
The Red Fort served his new capital, Shahjahanabad.

overview.text: Saladin, or Salah al-Din, was a Muslim ruler associated with the Ayyubid dynasty and the struggle against the Crusader states. His forces recaptured Jerusalem in October 1187, after advancing through Syria. That victory helped prompt the Third Crusade of 1189–92. During the crusade he confronted forces led by England’s Richard I, who won at Acre, Arsuf, and Jaffa; the two sides reached an agreement in 1192. Jerusalem remained under Saladin’s control while European pilgrims were allowed access. His career belongs to the histories of both Egypt and Syria as well as the crusades, and accounts of his conduct should be read in their specific political and religious settings.

His forces retook Jerusalem in October 1187.
The Third Crusade ran from 1189 to 1192.
Richard I fought Saladin’s forces at Acre, Arsuf, and Jaffa.
An agreement in 1192 followed Richard’s campaign.
